1.pericope_label: And if a soul sin, and hear the voice of swearing, and is a witness, whether he hath seen or known of it; if he do not utter it, then he shall bear his iniquity. Or if a soul touch any unclean thing, whether it be a carcase of an unclean beast, or a carcase of unclean cattle, or the carcase of unclean creeping things, and if it be hidden from him; he also shall be unclean, and guilty. Or if he touch the uncleanness of man, whatsoever uncleanness it be that a man shall be defiled withal, and it be hid from him; when he knoweth of it, then he shall be guilty. Or if a soul swear, pronouncing with his lips to do evil, or to do good, whatsoever it be that a man shall pronounce with an oath, and it be hid from him; when he knoweth of it, then he shall be guilty in one of these.

schools.summary: Place the chapter in its sequence, since the previous one gave the sin offering as it applies to the spiritual head, the congregation, the ruler and the private member, while this sets out the offering required when specific precepts have been violated; render the first case as failing to come forward after judicial adjuration has been uttered; take the rash oath as speech uttered heedlessly with the lips, in thoughtlessness or passion, and the pair to do evil or to do good as an idiom embracing all human action; and read the second case at its widest, any defilement whatever to which a man is exposed.

Admit at once that the three offences named look unlike one another, since concealing what one knows cannot arise from error, and explain how the first is nevertheless brought under that head: a man induced by shame or fear to connive at an offence he is questioned about blinds himself and withholds what he would have said had he examined the matter duly; then locate the fault of the broken vow not in the breaking but in the carelessness, since sound religion would have renewed the recollection, and where no anxiety to fulfil it appears there was no serious desire to do so.

Identify the thing heard as cursing or blasphemy or execration, whether against a neighbour or against God, on the ground that the crime must be of so high a nature that a hearer was bound to reveal it and prosecute the guilty; gloss the closing phrase as the punishment of iniquity rather than the iniquity itself; and state the dilemma of the rash vow plainly, that a man who vows an evil act would sin in keeping it yet is guilty for having made it, and a man who neglects the good he vowed is guilty too, so that either way he must confess and bring his offering.

Explain the judicial procedure that makes such silence possible, since judges among the Jews could adjure not only the witness but the suspected person, contrary to the rule that no man is bound to accuse himself — instancing the high priest adjuring the Saviour, who had stood silent until then and thereupon answered.

debates.question: What is the voice of swearing that the hearer must not conceal?

sides.position: A judicial adjuration, so that the offence is failing to come forward as a witness after it has been uttered
Cursing, blasphemy or execration, whether against a neighbour or against God, the crime being of so high a nature that a hearer was bound to prosecute it
A matter a man knew and concealed through shame or fear, which is brought under the head of error only by supposing he blinded himself

debates.question: Wherein lies the guilt of the rash oath?

sides.position: In the making of it, since a man who vows an evil act sins in keeping it yet is guilty for having sworn, and one who neglects the good he vowed is guilty too
In the carelessness rather than the breaking, since sound religion would have renewed the recollection of the vow
In heedless speech, an oath uttered in thoughtlessness or passion without the heart realising it

outliers.note: Alone explains the judicial machinery that made such silence an offence, noting that Jewish judges could adjure the suspected person as well as the witness, contrary to the rule that no man is bound to accuse himself, and instancing the high priest adjuring Christ.
Alone confronts the objection that concealing what one knows cannot be an error at all, and rescues the classification by supposing a man who blinds himself through shame or fear.

5.pericope_label: And it shall be, when he shall be guilty in one of these things, that he shall confess that he hath sinned in that thing: And he shall bring his trespass offering unto the Lord for his sin which he hath sinned, a female from the flock, a lamb or a kid of the goats, for a sin offering; and the priest shall make an atonement for him concerning his sin.

schools.summary: Note that the word here is properly trespass offering and is so rendered in thirty-five of the thirty-six places where it stands for a sacrifice; observe that in this section, unlike the sin offering of the previous chapter, no distinction is drawn between ranks of offender, so that the spiritual officer and the temporal sovereign stand level with the ordinary layman; render the victim as a sheep or a shaggy she-goat; and describe the ritual for the poor man's birds precisely, the head pinched off from opposite the neck without entirely severing it.

See a new principle beginning here in the distinction between rich and poor, which applies backwards as well and shows that the order of the chapter is not exactly kept, since the inserted cases interrupt the thread; and make the point of it that the poor are not to be pressed beyond their means, the grades of offering being appointed so that a man who could not manage two pigeons might be quit for a small measure of flour — from which it follows that the design was only to show the one true means of atonement.

Insist that restitution alone was not sufficient, since a man might restore without being much humbled while confession has a direct tendency to humble the soul, which is why the Scriptures require it so often; locate the confession before the Lord in the place of public worship and extend it by parity of reason to the other sacrifices for sin, of which it was a constant companion; and answer the difficulty that touching an unclean thing was elsewhere purged by simple washing, by taking this of a man who, being so unclean, then entered the tabernacle in ignorance.

debates.question: Why is confession required as well as restitution?

sides.position: Because restitution alone leaves a man unhumbled, while confession has a direct tendency to humble the soul, and without humiliation there can be no salvation
Because it belonged to the other sacrifices for sin as well, being a constant companion of them, and was to be made before the Lord in the place of public worship

outliers.note: Alone raises and answers the difficulty that touching an unclean thing was elsewhere purged by simple washing, taking this passage of a man who, being so unclean, then entered the tabernacle in ignorance.
Alone makes confession indispensable on psychological grounds, since a man may restore what he took without being humbled, and holds that without humiliation there can be no salvation.

7.pericope_label: And if he be not able to bring a lamb, then he shall bring for his trespass, which he hath committed, two turtledoves, or two young pigeons, unto the Lord; one for a sin offering, and the other for a burnt offering. And he shall bring them unto the priest, who shall offer that which is for the sin offering first, and wring off his head from his neck, but shall not divide it asunder: And he shall sprinkle of the blood of the sin offering upon the side of the altar; and the rest of the blood shall be wrung out at the bottom of the altar: it is a sin offering. And he shall offer the second for a burnt offering, according to the manner: and the priest shall make an atonement for him for his sin which he hath sinned, and it shall be forgiven him. But if he be not able to bring two turtledoves, or two young pigeons, then he that sinned shall bring for his offering the tenth part of an ephah of fine flour for a sin offering; he shall put no oil upon it, neither shall he put any frankincense thereon: for it is a sin offering. Then shall he bring it to the priest, and the priest shall take his handful of it, even a memorial thereof, and burn it on the altar, according to the offerings made by fire unto the Lord: it is a sin offering. And the priest shall make an atonement for him as touching his sin that he hath sinned in one of these, and it shall be forgiven him: and the remnant shall be the priest’s, as a meat offering.

schools.summary: Give poverty as the only ground on which the substitution is allowed, and explain why doves were chosen, being plentiful and cheap; answer the technical objection the substitution raises, that since the fat parts of a bird cannot be separated for the altar, and burning the whole would turn a trespass offering into a whole burnt offering, two doves were required so that one might serve each purpose; deny that the withholding of oil and frankincense is arbitrary, since the offering must be kept distinct from the meal offering; and strike the word remnant from the closing verse, which is not in the original, since apart from the handful burnt the whole tenth belonged to the priest.

Reckon the measures concretely, the tenth of an ephah at about three quarts or six pints, the whole ephah containing a little more than seven gallons and a half; note the order of the two birds, the sin offering first because it was for that particular sin and the burnt offering after because it was for sins in general, with the lesson that we are not to rest in general confessions; and give three reasons for the withholding of oil and frankincense — to distinguish the offering, to express sorrow by abstaining from pleasant things, and to signify that by sin a man deserves to lose both the oil of gladness and that acceptance of prayer which incense stands for.

Read the graduated offering as the most generous provision in the law, since the cost of the sin offering was brought lower than that of any other so that no man's poverty should ever bar his pardon, and the poorest of all may have atonement made for them if it be not their own fault — thus the poor are evangelized, and no man shall be able to say he had not wherewithal.

Take the lowest grade as supposing a man in the poorest circumstances he can well be, and find in the provision the grace of God, that atonement and forgiveness are provided for the poorest as well as for the rich; and read the burning of the handful as an emblem of the painful sufferings by which atonement was made.

debates.question: How large is the tenth part of an ephah?

sides.position: About three quarts, the whole ephah holding a little more than seven gallons and a half
A little less than half a gallon
About six pints

debates.question: Why must the flour offering have no oil or frankincense?

sides.position: To keep it distinct from the meal offering, since otherwise its character as a sin offering would be destroyed

For that reason, and also as an expression of sorrow by abstaining from pleasant things, and to signify that by sin a man deserves to lose the oil of gladness and the acceptance of prayer that incense stands for

outliers.note: Alone answers the technical objection that the fat of a bird cannot be separated for the altar, explaining that two doves were required so that one might serve for the altar and one for the offering proper.
Alone reads the graduated scale as the law evangelizing the poor, since the sin offering was made cheaper than any other so that no man could plead he had not wherewithal to obtain pardon.

themes: the tenth part of an ephah

14.pericope_label: And the Lord spake unto Moses, saying, If a soul commit a trespass, and sin through ignorance, in the holy things of the Lord; then he shall bring for his trespass unto the Lord a ram without blemish out of the flocks, with thy estimation by shekels of silver, after the shekel of the sanctuary, for a trespass offering: And he shall make amends for the harm that he hath done in the holy thing, and shall add the fifth part thereto, and give it unto the priest: and the priest shall make an atonement for him with the ram of the trespass offering, and it shall be forgiven him.

schools.summary: Argue the change of subject from the victim rather than the heading, since God now requires a male where before an ewe lamb or female kid sufficed, and a ram being more valuable it follows that a heavier offence is punished, the heinousness depending on the quality of the act when a man has wronged not a mortal but God himself; and include under the holy things both vows voluntarily made and the offering of a defective victim, anything by which God is defrauded of his right in an oblation.

Take the law to concern sacrilege and fraud in spiritual matters — the neglect to consecrate or redeem the firstborn, the withholding of firstfruits and tithes, the making of secular gain out of divine things, the keeping back of part of the price of what was dedicated; explain the estimation as valuing the defraud at the shekels it was worth or would sell for, paid down with a fifth part more and a ram besides, while admitting an obscurity in the text; and mark the boundary that makes the offering possible at all, since a man who did the thing knowingly was to be cut off.

Note that the introductory formula implies another communication made at a different time and a further development of the law; distinguish the word here rendered trespass from the one so rendered at the chapter's close, since this one means literally to cover and so to act covertly or faithlessly, used especially of a sacred covenant broken with God or between husband and wife; and set out the arithmetic of the added fifth as it was reckoned in the time of Christ, where the principal counted as four-fifths so that four shekels' worth cost five — by our reckoning a quarter rather than a fifth.

Mark the division of subject, that the preceding verses concerned offerings going by both names while here begin those that are properly and peculiarly trespass offerings, made to atone for wrongs done to a neighbour; and explain why the holy things form a distinct case, since a man who alienated them or converted them to his own use trespassed against the priests, to whose care they were entrusted and whose benefit they were.

debates.question: What counts as a trespass in the holy things?

sides.position: Sacrilege and fraud in spiritual matters — failing to redeem the firstborn, withholding firstfruits and tithes, making secular gain of divine things, keeping back part of the price of what was dedicated
Inadvertently keeping back what belongs to the sanctuary, the word used meaning literally to cover and so to act faithlessly under a sacred covenant
Vows voluntarily made, and the offering of a defective victim, and anything by which God is defrauded of his right in an oblation
Things consecrated to God and to holy uses, withheld or employed to some common use

debates.question: What is being estimated, and by whom?

sides.position: The defraud, valued at the shekels it was worth or would sell for, though there is an obscurity in the text
The damage done in the holy things, for which recompense was to be made as it was valued
The ram, at the priest's valuation — at present Moses', who was still performing the priest's part

outliers.note: Alone argues the change of subject from the sex of the victim, reasoning that a male is required where a female sufficed before, and that the greater value of the ram measures the greater heinousness of wronging God rather than a man.

Alone works the added fifth into figures, noting that by the reckoning current in the time of Christ the principal counted as four-fifths, so that what the text calls a fifth is by our arithmetic a quarter.

themes: the holy things of the Lord

17.pericope_label: And if a soul sin, and commit any of these things which are forbidden to be done by the commandments of the Lord; though he wist it not, yet is he guilty, and shall bear his iniquity. And he shall bring a ram without blemish out of the flock, with thy estimation, for a trespass offering, unto the priest: and the priest shall make an atonement for him concerning his ignorance wherein he erred and wist it not, and it shall be forgiven him. It is a trespass offering: he hath certainly trespassed against the Lord.

schools.summary: Weigh whether the expressions here are general, briefly confirming what has gone before, or restricted to particular cases, and come down for the second while allowing that a repetition would be no absurdity, since it would cut off every subterfuge from the disobedient; then take the reason added at the close to apply to every mode of expiation in the chapter, that a man who pretends ignorance, having sinned inconsiderately or contracted defilement through forgetfulness, is still guilty before God until he makes reconciliation.

Distinguish the two laws by their subject rather than by the offender's certainty, the former concerning the alienation of holy things from sacred to common use and this one other miscarriages about holy things and holy duties; then turn from the case to the reader, since given the purity of God and the breadth of his commandment it is no wonder that sinfulness is found in our holy things — but judge a second evil worse, the endeavour of religious people to reconcile themselves to that state and defend it as useful because it keeps them humble, whereas the more inward sin a man has the more pride he will feel.

Explain what makes this last case distinct, that the offering is required where a man only suspects he has put sacred property to his own use and can no longer remember which holy thing it was — which is why the exposition current during the second Temple called this the Doubtful Offering against the Certain Offering just above; improve two renderings, the estimation being Moses' valuation and the clause about not knowing meaning that he does not know the precise sacred thing; and draw the one substantial difference, that because the case is doubtful the offender is exempt from the additional fifth.

debates.question: Are the closing verses a general summary or a distinct case?

sides.position: A distinct case: the offering required where a man only suspects he has used sacred property and cannot remember which, called the Doubtful Offering against the Certain Offering above
Restricted to particular cases rather than general, though a repetition would be no absurdity since it would cut off subterfuge
A distinct subject: the former law concerned alienating holy things to common use, this one other miscarriages about holy things and holy duties

outliers.note: Alone turns from the case to the reader and attacks not the sinfulness found in holy things but the endeavour of religious people to defend that state as useful because it keeps them humble, answering that the more inward sin a man has the more pride he will feel.
Alone reports the rabbinic inference from the wording, that where an offering is said to be to the Lord it was not lawful for the priests to eat of it.
